y-m-25-01.title: Bike rental plans: which one is cheaper?
y-m-25-01.topic: Applying linear functions: the time when the graphs of two fare plans meet
y-m-25-01.goal: Compare two linear function models (fares) and say, with reasons, that which one is better can depend on the usage time.
y-m-25-01.material: The park bike rental station has two fare plans. Plan (가) charges a base fare of 1000원 at the start and then 100원 more for each minute of use. Plan (나) has no base fare and charges 150원 for each minute of use. The usage time is measured exactly in minutes (no rounding up or rounding off), and when the usage time is x minutes (x is 0 or more), the fare is y원.
y-m-25-01.thinking.0: Not generalizing from a single example
y-m-25-01.thinking.1: Revising your judgment and confidence with new information
y-m-25-01.thinking.2: Writing a conclusion with conditions attached
y-m-25-01.prereq.0: The meaning of the slope and the y-intercept in a linear function y=ax+b (grade 8 level)
y-m-25-01.prereq.1: Putting a value for x into an expression or table to find y
y-m-25-01.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose the most fitting thought using only what is known now, and when new information comes out, decide whether to keep or revise your judgment.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.hint.0: Compare how much the fare increases when time increases by 1 minute in each plan.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.hint.1: Fix several times and calculate the fares of the two plans side by side.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.0.info: All that is known now is the base fare and the per-minute fare of the two plans. We do not yet know how long Minji will ride the bike.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: Which plan will be cheaper for Minji? Choose the thoughts that fit with only what is known now (more than one thought may fit).
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.0.after: If you say 'always' without knowing the usage time, you are asserting even the cases you have not checked. The base fare and the per-minute fare favor opposite sides, so you can guess that it may depend on the time.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: (가), which has the lower per-minute fare, is always cheaper
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is a thought that looked only at the per-minute fare without considering the base fare.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It seems (나) for a short ride and (가) for a long ride, but we have to calculate to know
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You made a guess after seeing that the base fare and the per-minute fare each favor the opposite plan.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: (나), which has no base fare, is always cheaper
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is a thought that looked only at the base fare without considering the per-minute fare.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: If we do not know the usage time, we cannot decide which is cheaper
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is a careful judgment that holds off on a conclusion when information is lacking.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.1.info: Minji says she will ride for 10 minutes. The fares are (가) 100×10+1000=2000원 and (나) 150×10=1500원.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: Choose what fits as something you can say with this information (more than one may fit).
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.1.after: This information does not change your first judgment much. Now you have evidence that (나) is cheaper at 10 minutes, but the range that evidence reaches is only around 10 minutes.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: At 10 minutes, (나) is 500원 cheaper. For longer rides we cannot tell from this calculation alone
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You are seeing that whether the comparison at one time carries over to other times has to be checked separately.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: (나) is cheaper at 10 minutes, so (나) is cheaper at any time
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You asserted all cases from one example.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: (나) is cheaper at 10 minutes, so the shorter the ride, the better (가) gets
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You thought the opposite of the fact that the shorter the ride, the bigger the share the base fare takes up.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: If we look only at 10 minutes, we can recommend (나), and if the time changes we have to compare again
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You drew a conclusion only as far as the current evidence allows and left the rest open.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.2.info: This is the fare table on the station's notice board. 20 minutes: (가) 3000원, (나) 3000원 / 30 minutes: (가) 4000원, (나) 4500원.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: If Minji plans to ride for 40 minutes, which is cheaper and by how much? Choose the one that fits best, comparing with your earlier judgment.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.2.after: At 40 minutes, (가) is 5000원 and (나) is 6000원. At 20 minutes the two fares are equal; for shorter rides (나) is cheaper, and for longer rides (가) is cheaper.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: (나) is 1000원 cheaper. (나) was cheaper at 10 minutes, so it stays the same
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You brought the result at 10 minutes over to 40 minutes as it is.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: It seems you used the 500원 difference at 30 minutes in the table as it is for 40 minutes. If you calculate the 40-minute fare directly, it is different.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: (가) is 1000원 cheaper. After 20 minutes, the cheaper one changes
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You read that the cheaper plan switches around the time when the fares become equal.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The fares of the two plans are the same
y-m-25-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You applied the fact that they were equal at 20 minutes to other times.
y-m-25-01.s.s1.reflect: At 10 minutes (나) was cheaper, and at 40 minutes (가) was cheaper. Instead of saying 'always' from the comparison at one point in time, if you find the point at which the cheaper plan changes (the time when the two fares become equal), you can speak with conditions attached.
y-m-25-01.s.s2.prompt: Minji's friend also wants to use the same station but has not decided on a usage time yet. Write a recommendation with conditions about which plan would be good to pick.
y-m-25-01.s.s2.hint.0: Find the row on the notice board table where the two fares are equal.
y-m-25-01.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate once for a time shorter than that and once for a time longer than that, and turn them into sentences.
y-m-25-01.s.s2.placeholder: Example: if the usage time is ...
y-m-25-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you state the time at which the two plans become equal as a number?
y-m-25-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write without leaving out which is cheaper for short rides and for long rides?
y-m-25-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid assertive words like 'always'?
y-m-25-01.s.s2.model.0: If you ride for less than 20 minutes, (나) is cheaper, and if you ride for more than 20 minutes, (가) is cheaper. At exactly 20 minutes both are 3000원, the same.
y-m-25-01.s.s2.model.1: If you will ride for 20 minutes or less, choose (나), and if you will ride for more than 20 minutes, choose (가). At 20 minutes the fares are the same, so either is fine.

y-m-25-02.title: What measurements do we need to predict a spring's length?
y-m-25-02.topic: Determining the equation of a linear function: are the measurement records enough, and the range in which a prediction can be trusted
y-m-25-02.goal: Judge what information is needed to determine the equation of a linear function, and say how far a prediction made with that equation can be trusted.
y-m-25-02.material: In science class you do an experiment where you hang weights on a spring and measure the total length of the spring. Let the weight of the weights be x g and the total length of the spring be y cm. It is known that for this spring, up to 250 g, y is a linear function of x, y=ax+b (a is a nonzero number). Assume that all measurements were made on the same spring without error. Mina received sets of records measured by several groups.
y-m-25-02.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-25-02.thinking.1: Deciding for yourself what information is needed
y-m-25-02.thinking.2: Being aware of the range in which the equation holds
y-m-25-02.prereq.0: The meaning of a and b in a linear function y=ax+b
y-m-25-02.prereq.1: Reading the coordinates of a point on the coordinate plane
y-m-25-02.s.s1.prompt: Among the records below, choose all those from which, using that record alone, the equation y=ax+b of this spring can be determined as one. Nothing is known besides each record.
y-m-25-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each set of records, count how many different weights there are.
y-m-25-02.s.s1.hint.1: Write each set's records as (weight, length) points and imagine how many straight lines pass through all those points.
y-m-25-02.s.s1.o.a: The case where there is only one record, 10 cm at 0 g
y-m-25-02.s.s1.r.a: You may not have seen that if there is only one point, several lines pass through it.
y-m-25-02.s.s1.o.b: 12 cm at 50 g, 14 cm at 100 g
y-m-25-02.s.s1.r.b: This is a judgment that looked at how much the length changes between two different weights.
y-m-25-02.s.s1.o.c: A record measuring 14 cm at 100 g twice (14 cm both times)
y-m-25-02.s.s1.r.c: This is a judgment that saw many measurements as enough. You did not count how many different weights there are.
y-m-25-02.s.s1.o.d: 12 cm at 50 g, 16 cm at 150 g
y-m-25-02.s.s1.r.d: This is a judgment that saw that records at two places far apart in weight also tell the change.
y-m-25-02.s.s1.o.e: 10 cm at 0 g, 18 cm at 200 g
y-m-25-02.s.s1.r.e: This is a judgment that saw that the length with no weight hung can also be used as one point.
y-m-25-02.s.s1.explain: The equation of a linear function is determined as one if there are records at two points with different x. If there is only one point, or the same weight was measured many times, several lines pass through that point, so it cannot be determined.
y-m-25-02.s.s2.prompt: The same equation y=0.04x+10 came out from the records of b, d, and e (x in g, y in cm). The spring's manual says only 'up to 250 g, the length is a linear function of the weight'. When Mina put x=300 into this equation and predicted y=22 cm, how should this prediction be treated?
y-m-25-02.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the range of weights written in the manual with the weight you want to predict.
y-m-25-02.s.s2.hint.1: Think of the interval confirmed by the experiment or manual and the interval that is not confirmed separately.
y-m-25-02.s.s2.o.a: I calculated it with the equation, so it is fine to write that the length at 300 g is 22 cm
y-m-25-02.s.s2.r.a: You trusted the value as it is without checking the range in which the equation holds.
y-m-25-02.s.s2.o.b: It goes beyond the range in the manual, so I think this equation cannot be used at all
y-m-25-02.s.s2.r.b: You threw away the whole equation without distinguishing values outside the range from values inside the range.
y-m-25-02.s.s2.o.c: State that outside 250 g there is no guarantee, so 22 cm is only a prediction
y-m-25-02.s.s2.r.c: You are speaking of the range where the equation is confirmed and the range where it is not separately.
y-m-25-02.s.s2.o.d: It is only a little over 250 g, so the error is small and it is fine to write 22 cm
y-m-25-02.s.s2.r.d: You thought a small deviation is fine, but no grounds for that were given.
y-m-25-02.s.s2.explain: The equation is guaranteed only inside the confirmed range. A value beyond 250 g is only a prediction under the condition 'if this equation keeps holding'. For values inside the range (for example, 120 g) you may predict with the equation.
y-m-25-02.s.s3.prompt: The group that has the first set of records (only one record, 10 cm at 0 g) can make exactly one more measurement. Write what to measure so that the equation can be determined, and why that measurement helps.
y-m-25-02.s.s3.hint.0: Think about what changes if you measure at a weight different from the weight of the point you already have.
y-m-25-02.s.s3.hint.1: Write the weight difference and the length difference of the two points.
y-m-25-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the weight you newly measure different from 0 g?
y-m-25-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write the reason why that measurement helps?
y-m-25-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write specifically exactly which values are needed (weight and length)?
y-m-25-02.s.s3.model.0: Hang a weight other than 0 g, for example 100 g, and measure the length. Then there are two points, so I can find how much the length increases when the weight increases, that is, the slope.
y-m-25-02.s.s3.model.1: Hang one more weight and measure the length at a weight different from 0 g. Comparing how much the length changed with how much the weight changed tells me the slope.

y-m-25-03.title: The equation that passes through both points: can we trust it?
y-m-25-03.topic: Equation of a line through two points: independence of a check, and errors in a solution
y-m-25-03.goal: Examine whether a check is independent of the information used to make the equation, find the first wrong line in the solution, and make points on the corrected equation.
y-m-25-03.material: Minsu tried to write the line through the two points A(2, 3) and B(6, 11) on the coordinate plane as an equation of the form y=ax+b. The equation Minsu found is y=(1/2)x+2. Minsu says he finished checking by 'putting in point A(2, 3), (1/2)×2+2=3, so it's right'.
y-m-25-03.thinking.0: Evaluating the grounds for a check
y-m-25-03.thinking.2: Checking the corrected result with points
y-m-25-03.prereq.0: The meaning of the slope a in a linear function y=ax+b
y-m-25-03.prereq.1: How to check by putting a point's coordinates into the equation to see if it holds
y-m-25-03.s.s1.prompt: The equation Minsu found is y=(1/2)x+2 (read aloud: y equals one-half x plus 2), and he says it worked when he put in the point A(2, 3). Can you be sure the equation is right from this alone? Choose the most fitting judgment.
y-m-25-03.s.s1.hint.0: Recall which of the points A and B Minsu probably used, and how, when making the equation.
y-m-25-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether a check has meaning only when it is done with information that was not used to make the equation.
y-m-25-03.s.s1.o.a: It worked at A, so you can be sure the equation is right and there is no need to check more
y-m-25-03.s.s1.r.a: You did not consider whether the point used for the check overlaps with the information used to make the equation.
y-m-25-03.s.s1.o.b: A is a point used to make the equation, so you should also put in B(6, 11)
y-m-25-03.s.s1.r.b: You thought a check has meaning only when it is done with information that was not used to make the equation.
y-m-25-03.s.s1.o.c: It worked at A, but it must be wrong at B, so the equation should be thrown away
y-m-25-03.s.s1.r.c: You asserted it was wrong before even putting it in.
y-m-25-03.s.s1.explain: It can be natural for it to work at a point used to make the equation. You can know whether the equation passes through both points only by checking with a point not yet used (or with another method).
y-m-25-03.s.s2.prompt: When B(6, 11) was put in, Minsu's equation turned out to be wrong. Choose the first wrong line in Minsu's solution (line numbers start from 1 as they appear on the screen).
y-m-25-03.s.s2.hint.0: Before redoing the calculation of each line, work backward from the fact that putting in B shows it is wrong.
y-m-25-03.s.s2.hint.1: Find yourself the amount x increases and the amount y increases between the two points, and compare with line 2.
y-m-25-03.s.s2.line.0: Let the equation of the line through A(2, 3) and B(6, 11) be y = ax + b.
y-m-25-03.s.s2.line.1: Slope a = (increase in x) ÷ (increase in y) = (6−2) ÷ (11−3) = 4/8 = 1/2
y-m-25-03.s.s2.line.2: Putting A(2, 3) into y = (1/2)x + b gives 3 = 1 + b, so b = 2
y-m-25-03.s.s2.line.3: So the equation we want is y = (1/2)x + 2
y-m-25-03.s.s2.explain: It is line 2. The slope is (increase in y) ÷ (increase in x), so (11−3) ÷ (6−2) = 8/4 = 2. Lines 3 and 4 are the results of continuing with the wrong slope. The correct equation is y = 2x − 1, and when B(6, 11) is put in, 12 − 1 = 11 holds.
y-m-25-03.s.s3.prompt: Find 3 different points that lie on the correct equation and are not A or B, and enter them as (x, y). However, x is from −10 to 10.
y-m-25-03.s.s3.hint.0: Find how much y increases when x increases by 4 from A to B.
y-m-25-03.s.s3.hint.1: Starting from A, find the points one by one using how much y changes each time x increases by 1.
y-m-25-03.s.s3.ok.c1: This point lies on the line through A and B.
y-m-25-03.s.s3.fail.c1: This point does not lie on the line through A and B. Compare the ratio of the increase in x to the increase in y from A to this point with that of AB.
y-m-25-03.s.s3.ok.c2: It is a point different from A and B.
y-m-25-03.s.s3.fail.c2: It is the same point as A or B. Find a different point.
y-m-25-03.s.s3.explain: Example: (0, −1), (1, 1), (4, 7). All are points on y = 2x − 1. There is only one line through two points, so with the correct equation, any x gives a point on the same line. The point (4, 4) on Minsu's equation y = (1/2)x + 2 is not on this line.

y-m-25-04.title: Even if two equations look different, is there just one solution?
y-m-25-04.topic: Solutions of simultaneous linear equations and the positions of two lines (one solution, none, infinitely many)
y-m-25-04.goal: Understand that two linear equations that look different can be the same line, sort out the cases where the number of solutions depends on a constant, and make equations of the same line yourself.
y-m-25-04.material: In simultaneous equations, a linear equation ax+by=c can be drawn as a line on the coordinate plane (a and b are not both 0). If two lines meet at one point, there is one pair of solutions; if they do not meet, there is no solution; and if they overlap completely, there are infinitely many solutions. A pair (x, y) that satisfies both equations is called a solution of the simultaneous equations.
y-m-25-04.thinking.1: Stating conclusions that depend on conditions
y-m-25-04.prereq.0: Seeing the solutions of a linear equation ax+by=c as points on the coordinate plane
y-m-25-04.prereq.1: The meaning of the slope and the y-intercept of a line
y-m-25-04.s.s1.prompt: How many pairs (x, y) satisfy both the first equation 2x − y = −1 (read aloud: 2x minus y equals negative 1) and the second equation 4x − 2y = −2?
y-m-25-04.s.s1.hint.0: Rewrite each equation in the form y = (slope)x + (y-intercept) and write them side by side.
y-m-25-04.s.s1.hint.1: Put x = 0 and x = 1 into both equations, find the values of y, and compare them.
y-m-25-04.s.s1.o.a: There is only one pair. Because the two equations have different forms
y-m-25-04.s.s1.r.a: You thought that if the equations look different, they are different lines.
y-m-25-04.s.s1.o.b: There is no pair. Because the two lines have the same slope, so they are parallel
y-m-25-04.s.s1.r.b: You looked only at the slopes being equal and did not compare the y-intercepts.
y-m-25-04.s.s1.o.c: There are infinitely many. Because the two equations represent the same line
y-m-25-04.s.s1.r.c: You saw that even if the appearance differs, they can be the same line.
y-m-25-04.s.s1.explain: If you divide both sides of 4x − 2y = −2 by 2, you get 2x − y = −1. The two equations are the same line, so every point on the line is a solution.
y-m-25-04.s.s2.prompt: Keep the first equation as it is, and change the second equation to 4x − 2y = c (c is a constant). How does the number of solutions change depending on the value of c?
y-m-25-04.s.s2.hint.0: Put a few numbers (for example, −2, 0, 4) in for c and compare the y-intercepts of the two lines.
y-m-25-04.s.s2.hint.1: Separate the cases where the two lines have the same slope into those with the same y-intercept and those with different y-intercepts.
y-m-25-04.s.s2.o.a: Whatever c is, there are infinitely many solutions. Because the coefficients are the same
y-m-25-04.s.s2.r.a: You looked only at the coefficients of the equation and did not consider the constant term c.
y-m-25-04.s.s2.o.b: Only for one c are there infinitely many solutions, and for the rest there is no solution
y-m-25-04.s.s2.r.b: You saw that when c changes, the line moves in parallel.
y-m-25-04.s.s2.o.c: Only for one c is there no solution, and for the other c there is one pair each
y-m-25-04.s.s2.r.c: You thought that if the slopes are equal, the lines meet in every case.
y-m-25-04.s.s2.o.d: If c is not 0, there is always one pair, and if it is 0, there is none
y-m-25-04.s.s2.explain: 4x − 2y = c is y = 2x − c/2, and the first equation is y = 2x + 1. The slopes are the same, so they are the same line only when c = −2, and for other c they are parallel and do not overlap, so there is no solution.
y-m-25-04.s.s3.prompt: Make a second equation ax + by = c that represents the same line as the first equation 2x − y = −1. So that the appearance is not the same, a must not be 2, and enter 3 different equations as (a, b, c).
y-m-25-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write down the coefficients 2, −1, −1 of the first equation and put them side by side with a, b, c of the second equation.
y-m-25-04.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether the two equations pass through the same points when x = 0 and when y = 0.
y-m-25-04.s.s3.ok.c1: The ratio of the coefficients of x and y is the same as in the first equation, so the slope is the same.
y-m-25-04.s.s3.fail.c1: The ratio of the coefficients of x and y is different from the first equation, so the slope is different.
y-m-25-04.s.s3.ok.c2: The constant term is in the same ratio too, so the lines overlap.
y-m-25-04.s.s3.fail.c2: The ratio of the coefficients is right but the constant term is not in that ratio, so it is a different parallel line.
y-m-25-04.s.s3.ok.c3: Its appearance is different from the first equation.
y-m-25-04.s.s3.fail.c3: a is 2 or 0. Its appearance is the same as the first equation, or it does not make a line.
y-m-25-04.s.s3.explain: Example: (4, −2, −2), (−2, 1, 1), (6, −3, −3). If the three numbers of the second equation are the three numbers (2, −1, −1) of the first equation multiplied by the same number, the two equations are the same line. If even one number departs from that ratio, it is not the same line.

y-m-25-05.title: Is the one with the bigger slope number faster?
y-m-25-05.topic: Reading the slope of a graph: comparing two graphs with different units
y-m-25-05.goal: Understand that a slope must be read together with its units, and compare two graphs with different units by converting them to the same units.
y-m-25-05.material: Doyun and Seoa each walk at a constant speed, and they drew their records as graphs. Doyun's graph has time (minutes) on the horizontal axis and distance walked (m) on the vertical axis, and it is a line through the origin (0, 0) and the point (10, 700). Seoa's graph has time (hours) on the horizontal axis and distance walked (km) on the vertical axis, and it is a line through the origin and the point (2, 10).
y-m-25-05.thinking.1: Converting to the same units to compare
y-m-25-05.thinking.2: Knowing the assumption that makes the comparison valid
y-m-25-05.prereq.0: The meaning of the slope a in the graph of a linear function y=ax
y-m-25-05.s.s1.prompt: Doyun said, 'The slope of my graph is 70 and Seoa's is 5, so I'm much faster!' How would you judge this statement?
y-m-25-05.s.s1.hint.0: For each graph, say how much the vertical axis increases when the horizontal axis increases by 1, together with the unit.
y-m-25-05.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the units attached to the two slopes are the same.
y-m-25-05.s.s1.o.a: The units of the two graphs are different, so they cannot be compared by the numbers alone
y-m-25-05.s.s1.r.a: You read the meaning of the slope together with its unit.
y-m-25-05.s.s1.o.b: The bigger the slope, the faster, so Doyun, whose 70 is bigger than 5, is faster
y-m-25-05.s.s1.r.b: You compared only the sizes of the numbers without checking the units.
y-m-25-05.s.s1.o.c: The smaller the slope, the sooner you cover the same distance, so Seoa is faster
y-m-25-05.s.s1.r.c: You thought the relationship between slope and speed the wrong way around.
y-m-25-05.s.s1.explain: The slope is the amount the vertical axis increases when the horizontal axis increases by 1. Doyun goes 70 m per minute and Seoa goes 5 km per hour, so if the units are different, they cannot be compared by the numbers alone.
y-m-25-05.s.s2.prompt: If you change Doyun's walking to the same units as Seoa's graph (hours on the horizontal axis, km on the vertical axis), Doyun goes d km in t hours. Enter 3 different pairs (t, d) that fit this relationship. However, 0 < t ≤ 3.
y-m-25-05.s.s2.hint.0: Find the distance Doyun goes in 1 minute, and then find the distance he goes in 1 hour.
y-m-25-05.s.s2.hint.1: Change the distance you got from m to km, fix a few times, and calculate the distances.
y-m-25-05.s.s2.ok.c1: The time is within the range.
y-m-25-05.s.s2.fail.c1: t is not greater than 0 and at most 3.
y-m-25-05.s.s2.fail.c2: It does not fit Doyun's walking. Doyun goes 700 m in 10 minutes, and 1 hour is 60 minutes and 1 km is 1000 m.
y-m-25-05.s.s2.explain: Doyun goes 700 m in 10 minutes, that is, 70 m in 1 minute. In 1 hour (60 minutes), it is 4200 m = 4.2 km, so points like (1, 4.2), (2, 8.4), (0.5, 2.1) all fit.
y-m-25-05.s.s2.because.prompt: In one or two sentences, write how you found (t, d).
y-m-25-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: First write in a sentence the relationship between 1 minute and 1 hour.
y-m-25-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Next write the relationship between m and km.
y-m-25-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Can you see the process of changing the time unit?
y-m-25-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Can you see the process of changing the distance unit?
y-m-25-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Can you follow where the last value came from?
y-m-25-05.s.s2.because.model.0: It's 700 m in 10 minutes, so it's 70 m in 1 minute. 1 hour is 60 minutes, so 70×60=4200 m, and 1000 m is 1 km, so it's 4.2 km.
y-m-25-05.s.s2.because.model.1: 700 m is 0.7 km and 10 minutes is 1/6 hour. For 1 hour, he goes 0.7×6=4.2 km.
y-m-25-05.s.s3.prompt: It means Doyun walks 4.2 km per hour and Seoa walks 5 km per hour. For this comparison to be meaningful, what assumption is absolutely necessary?
y-m-25-05.s.s3.hint.0: Think about whether, if the graph bends or curves, you could still state 'how many km per hour' as a single number.
y-m-25-05.s.s3.hint.1: Work out one by one whether each choice is information needed to find the speed.
y-m-25-05.s.s3.o.a: We measured the distance the two walked during the same time
y-m-25-05.s.s3.r.a: You thought the distances over the same time must be compared. It is not needed to compare speeds.
y-m-25-05.s.s3.o.b: The two walked the same road in the same direction
y-m-25-05.s.s3.r.b: You thought it had to be the same road, but the shape of the road does not matter for comparing speeds.
y-m-25-05.s.s3.o.c: The two started from the same place at the same time
y-m-25-05.s.s3.r.c: You thought the starting point must be the same, but speed has nothing to do with the starting point.
y-m-25-05.s.s3.o.d: Both walked at a constant speed
y-m-25-05.s.s3.r.d: You saw that only for a straight-line graph is the slope the speed.
y-m-25-05.s.s3.explain: If the graph is a straight line, it means the speed is constant, so the slope is the speed. The same time, the same road, and the same starting point are not needed.

y-m-25-06.title: If the areas are the same, are the slopes the same too?
y-m-25-06.topic: The triangle enclosed by the graph of a linear function and the two axes: same area, different slopes
y-m-25-06.goal: Refute the generalization 'if the areas are the same, the slopes are the same' with a counterexample, and work out how the conclusion changes when the condition is changed.
y-m-25-06.material: On the coordinate plane there is a line whose x-intercept is a and whose y-intercept is b (a and b are nonzero numbers). This line passes through the points (a, 0) and (0, b) and forms a triangle together with the x-axis and the y-axis. The area of this triangle is half of the product of the absolute value of a and the absolute value of b. Hyeonu says, 'Lines that form triangles of the same area with the two axes also have the same slope.'
y-m-25-06.thinking.0: Deciding the shape of a counterexample
y-m-25-06.thinking.2: Changing a condition and judging again
y-m-25-06.prereq.0: The meaning of the x-intercept, y-intercept, and slope in the graph of a linear function
y-m-25-06.prereq.1: Finding the area of a right triangle
y-m-25-06.s.s1.prompt: You want to test whether Hyeonu's statement 'lines that form triangles of the same area with the two axes also have the same slope' is always true. What two lines would you need to find to show that this statement is wrong?
y-m-25-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write down separately the 'condition' (the areas are the same) and the 'conclusion' (the slopes are the same) in Hyeonu's statement.
y-m-25-06.s.s1.hint.1: Say what an example that keeps the condition but breaks the conclusion would look like.
y-m-25-06.s.s1.o.a: Two lines with different areas and the same slope
y-m-25-06.s.s1.r.a: You thought of the direction of the claim the wrong way around (slope to area).
y-m-25-06.s.s1.o.b: Two lines with the same area and the same slope
y-m-25-06.s.s1.r.b: You missed that finding an example where the claim holds only confirms the claim.
y-m-25-06.s.s1.o.c: Two lines with the same area and different slopes
y-m-25-06.s.s1.r.c: You saw that an example that satisfies the condition of the claim and breaks the conclusion is a counterexample.
y-m-25-06.s.s1.o.d: Two lines with different areas and different slopes
y-m-25-06.s.s1.r.d: You missed that an example that does not satisfy the condition of the claim (the areas are the same) is not a test.
y-m-25-06.s.s1.explain: To break the statement that 'if A, then B' is always true, you only need one example that satisfies A but breaks B. Here that is two lines with the same area and different slopes.
y-m-25-06.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 lines whose triangle has area 12 and whose slopes are all different. For each line, enter the x-intercept a and the y-intercept b. At this step, a and b are both positive.
y-m-25-06.s.s2.hint.0: First write as an expression what value made from a and b must equal what for the area to be 12.
y-m-25-06.s.s2.hint.1: Fix a first and adjust b, then check yourself that the slopes do not overlap.
y-m-25-06.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b are not both positive.
y-m-25-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The area of the triangle is 12.
y-m-25-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The area of the triangle (half the product of a and b) is not 12.
y-m-25-06.s.s2.explain: Example: (4, 6), (6, 4), (3, 8). All have area 12 but the slopes differ: −3/2, −2/3, −8/3. So Hyeonu's statement is not always true.
y-m-25-06.s.s2.because.prompt: Write your answer to Hyeonu's statement in one or two sentences, using the examples above as evidence.
y-m-25-06.s.s2.because.hint.0: You may use the intercepts of the two lines you made above as they are.
y-m-25-06.s.s2.because.hint.1: First write in one sentence 'why Hyeonu's statement is wrong'.
y-m-25-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check that in the examples you gave, the areas are the same and the slopes are different?
y-m-25-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write knowing that one example is enough?
y-m-25-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you write how the word 'always' gets broken?
y-m-25-06.s.s2.because.model.0: Hyeonu's statement is wrong. For example, if a=4, b=6 the area is 12, and if a=6, b=4 the area is also 12, but the slopes are different from each other.
y-m-25-06.s.s2.because.model.1: It is not always so. The line with intercepts (4, 6) and the line with intercepts (3, 8) both have area 12 but different slopes, so they are a counterexample.
y-m-25-06.s.s3.prompt: Now change the condition. How many lines have slope −3/2 (read aloud: negative three halves) and form a triangle of area 12 with the two axes? This time there is no assumption that the two intercepts are positive.
y-m-25-06.s.s3.hint.0: Write the line with slope −3/2 as y = −(3/2)x + k, and find where it meets the two axes when k is 6 and when k is −6.
y-m-25-06.s.s3.hint.1: Find the area of the triangle in each of the two cases and check whether it is 12.
y-m-25-06.s.s3.o.a: One: only the line with intercepts (4, 0) and (0, 6), and there is no other
y-m-25-06.s.s3.r.a: You carried over the assumption of positive intercepts from the previous step as it is.
y-m-25-06.s.s3.o.b: Two: one line with positive intercepts and one with negative intercepts
y-m-25-06.s.s3.r.b: You did not miss that a line with negative intercepts has the same area too.
y-m-25-06.s.s3.o.c: None: because once the slope is fixed, the area is fixed too
y-m-25-06.s.s3.r.c: You thought the slope alone fixes the area.
y-m-25-06.s.s3.o.d: Infinitely many: any line is possible as long as the slope is the same
y-m-25-06.s.s3.r.d: You did not consider how many lines the area condition narrows it down to.
y-m-25-06.s.s3.explain: A line with slope −3/2 has the form y = −(3/2)x + k. The area then is k²/3, and for it to be 12, k is 6 or −6. So there are two: y = −(3/2)x + 6 and y = −(3/2)x − 6.

y-m-25-07.title: What numbers must a and b be for the line not to pass through the second quadrant?
y-m-25-07.topic: The quadrants a linear function's graph passes through, and the signs of the slope and y-intercept
y-m-25-07.goal: Find the condition for a line not to pass through the second quadrant using the signs of the slope and y-intercept, without missing the boundary (the case where the y-intercept is 0).
y-m-25-07.material: The graph of a linear function y=ax+b is a line (a is a nonzero number). a is the slope and b is the y-intercept. The second quadrant is the region of points whose x-coordinate is negative and whose y-coordinate is positive. Points on the x-axis or the y-axis do not belong to any quadrant.
y-m-25-07.thinking.0: Testing with examples to find a condition
y-m-25-07.thinking.2: Finding the error in a summary
y-m-25-07.prereq.0: The meaning of the slope and the y-intercept in a linear function y=ax+b
y-m-25-07.prereq.1: The position of the quadrants (second quadrant: x<0, y>0)
y-m-25-07.s.s1.prompt: Among the following lines, choose all that do not pass through the second quadrant.
y-m-25-07.s.s1.hint.0: For each equation, calculate what y is when x is −1 and −10.
y-m-25-07.s.s1.hint.1: Look for a place where y becomes positive when x is negative.
y-m-25-07.s.s1.r.a: You recalled the position of a line with a positive slope and a negative y-intercept.
y-m-25-07.s.s1.r.b: You thought that if the y-intercept is negative, a line going to the upper left also avoids the second quadrant.
y-m-25-07.s.s1.r.c: You missed that if the y-intercept is positive, even going left it is still in the upper part.
y-m-25-07.s.s1.r.d: You thought a line through the origin does not pass through any quadrant.
y-m-25-07.s.s1.r.e: You know that even a line through the origin passes through only one pair of quadrants.
y-m-25-07.s.s1.explain: The second quadrant is the region x < 0, y > 0. For y = 3x − 2 and y = 2x, y is negative (or 0) when x is negative, so they do not enter this region. For the rest, y becomes positive somewhere where x is negative.
y-m-25-07.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different (a, b) for linear functions y = ax + b that do not pass through the second quadrant. a is the slope and b is the y-intercept.
y-m-25-07.s.s2.hint.0: Make the slope positive, change the y-intercept, and check whether y becomes positive at x = −1 and −10.
y-m-25-07.s.s2.hint.1: Test the case where the y-intercept is 0 and the case where it is negative separately.
y-m-25-07.s.s2.ok.c1: The sign of the slope is suitable.
y-m-25-07.s.s2.fail.c1: With this slope, y becomes positive somewhere where x is small enough, or it is not a linear function. Check the sign of the slope again.
y-m-25-07.s.s2.ok.c2: The range of the y-intercept is suitable.
y-m-25-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The y-intercept is large, so even a little to the left above the y-axis, y is positive. Check the range of the y-intercept again.
y-m-25-07.s.s2.explain: Example: (3, −2), (2, 0), (0.5, −4). If the slope is positive and the y-intercept is 0 or less, the line passes through only the first and third quadrants (and the fourth quadrant too if the y-intercept is negative).
y-m-25-07.s.s3.prompt: A student summarized the results above with reasons. Choose the wrong line (line numbers start from 1 as they appear on the screen).
y-m-25-07.s.s3.hint.0: Check the line with b = 0 (for example, y = 2x) at a place where x is negative.
y-m-25-07.s.s3.hint.1: Look for an example among those you made in step 2 that does not agree with this summary.
y-m-25-07.s.s3.line.0: If a < 0, y becomes positive somewhere where x is small enough, so the line passes through the second quadrant. So a must be > 0.
y-m-25-07.s.s3.line.1: If a > 0 and b > 0, then moving just a little to the left from the point (0, b), y is positive, so it passes through the second quadrant.
y-m-25-07.s.s3.line.2: If b = 0 it passes through the origin, but in this case there is no y-intercept, so only b < 0 is possible.
y-m-25-07.s.s3.line.3: Summary: it does not pass through the second quadrant only when a > 0 and b < 0.
y-m-25-07.s.s3.explain: It is lines 3 and 4. A line through the origin also has a y-intercept, which is 0 (b = 0). If a > 0 and b = 0, this line does not pass through the second quadrant. So the summary is a > 0 and b ≤ 0.

y-m-25-08.title: Until when can we trust the equation y=−5x+200?
y-m-25-08.topic: The range in which a linear function model holds: when the situation changes, the equation changes too
y-m-25-08.goal: Check the range and conditions in which a linear function equation holds, and understand that the equation can change when the situation changes, revising your judgment with new information.
y-m-25-08.material: When you open the drain valve of a tank holding 200 L of water, water drains out at 5 L per minute. Call the moment the valve is opened 0 minutes, and let the amount of water left in the tank after x minutes be y L. Look at 0 minutes to 60 minutes. The water in the tank cannot go below 0 L.
y-m-25-08.thinking.0: Working out whether the value of an expression has meaning in the situation
y-m-25-08.thinking.1: Revising your judgment with new information
y-m-25-08.thinking.2: Dividing up the situation and setting up the model again
y-m-25-08.prereq.0: Putting an x value into a linear function y=ax+b to find y
y-m-25-08.prereq.1: What it means when y decreases because the slope is negative
y-m-25-08.s.s1.prompt: Look at the situation of water draining from the tank as information is added one piece at a time. At each step, choose the most fitting thought.
y-m-25-08.s.s1.hint.0: Put in a value for x to find y, and then check whether that value has meaning in the situation.
y-m-25-08.s.s1.hint.1: Divide the time at the moment when the situation changed.
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.0.info: This is the first situation. The valve is kept open, and the amount of water left is expressed as y = −5x + 200 (0 ≤ x ≤ 40).
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.0.ask: How much water is left in the tank after 30 minutes?
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.0.after: y = −5×30 + 200 = 50 L. It is a value within the range where the equation holds (0 ≤ x ≤ 40).
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You read the amount that drained out as the amount left.
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You put the time into the equation and found the amount left.
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It cannot be known from the given information
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You did not see that the value can be found even though the equation was given.
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.1.info: If you put x = 50 into the equation, y = −50 comes out. But this tank drains completely and becomes empty after 40 minutes.
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.1.ask: How should the value y = −50 be read?
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.1.after: The equation can be calculated, but in the situation the water cannot be less than 0 L. The range in which the equation can be trusted is 0 ≤ x ≤ 40.
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.1.o.a: After 50 minutes there is −50 L of water in the tank
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You read the value of the equation as the value in the situation.
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The equation is wrong, so it must not be used
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Because of one value outside the range, you threw away even the values inside the range.
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The equation fits the situation only up to 40 minutes, and after that the water left is 0 L
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You looked at the range in which the equation holds and the limit of the situation together.
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.2.info: This is new information. The manager closed the valve at 20 minutes and opened it again at 25 minutes (the draining speed after reopening is the same).
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.2.ask: How much water is left in the tank after 30 minutes? How should the 50 L you first found be corrected?
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.2.after: At 20 minutes 100 L is left, and it stays that way until 25 minutes. From 25 minutes it drains 5 L at a time, so at 30 minutes it is 100 − 25 = 75 L.
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 50 L: the equation y = −5x + 200 can be used from start to finish
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You thought the first equation stays right even when the situation changes.
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 100 L: after it was closed, no more drains out
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You missed the draining after it was reopened.
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 25 L: water drained during the 5 minutes it was closed too
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You thought water drained even while it was closed.
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.2.o.d: 75 L: the 25 L that did not drain during the 5 minutes the valve was closed remains extra
y-m-25-08.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You calculated that it drained less by the length of time it was closed.
y-m-25-08.s.s1.reflect: At first you found the value at 30 minutes correctly with the equation, but after the situation changed, the same equation no longer fit. You have to check under what conditions the equation was made and whether those conditions continue to hold.
y-m-25-08.s.s2.prompt: The valve was closed at 20 minutes and opened again at 25 minutes (the draining speed is the same). Enter 3 different times x minutes at which the actual amount of water left differs from the value of the equation y = −5x + 200, together with the water left y L at that time, as (x, y). However, 20 < x ≤ 60.
y-m-25-08.s.s2.hint.0: Write the water left at 20 minutes, 25 minutes, and 30 minutes in order.
y-m-25-08.s.s2.hint.1: Count separately only the time that water actually drained.
y-m-25-08.s.s2.ok.c1: The time is within the range.
y-m-25-08.s.s2.fail.c1: x is not greater than 20 and at most 60.
y-m-25-08.s.s2.ok.c2: It is the actual amount of water left at that time.
y-m-25-08.s.s2.fail.c2: It is not the actual amount of water left at that time. Divide the time into when the valve was open and when it was closed.
y-m-25-08.s.s2.explain: From 20 to 25 minutes it stays at 100 L. From 25 minutes it is y = 100 − 5(x − 25) = 225 − 5x, and if it becomes empty at 45 minutes, after that it is 0 L. After 20 minutes, the values differ from the first equation.
